title: Lennon-McCartney and the concentration of songwriting
text:
There were four Beatles. Two of them wrote 88% of the songs.
I went through the catalogue and counted the credits. Lennon and McCartney are on roughly 180 songs. George Harrison wrote about 22. Ringo Starr wrote 2. So of every original the band recorded, almost nine in ten carry the Lennon-McCartney name.



Chart of songwriting credit shares among Beatles members


Here is why that goes beyond trivia. A songwriting credit is its own income stream. When the band plays a show, the performance fees get split. But the writer’s share of a song’s royalties goes to the people credited as writers, not to everyone who played on it. For Lennon-McCartney songs, that meant John and Paul, not George and Ringo.
That gap shaped the band. Harrison spent years frustrated that his songs had to fight for room on each album. When he finally got the space, he turned in “Something” and “Here Comes the Sun,” two of the most covered songs the Beatles ever released. The talent was never the constraint. Access to the catalogue was.
And here is the twist that makes the point sharper. Writing a song and owning it are two different rights. Lennon and McCartney wrote the catalogue, then lost control of who owned it. The publishing company was sold, changed hands, and in 1985 Michael Jackson bought it for 47.5 million dollars, outbidding McCartney for his own songs. So even the writers did not end up holding their work — that saga gets its own post.
This is the part people miss about creative businesses. Value does not accrue to whoever is in the room. It accrues along the rights, and the rights were never split evenly.
I look at concentration for a living. In any market, two of four players holding 88% of the output would catch my eye. The Beatles just made that concentration sound like the best decade of music ever recorded.
So what is your read. Was the Lennon-McCartney lock fair to Harrison, or simply the deal he agreed to?
Code and data: github.com/taniseb/beatlenomics

title: Did Get Back move the catalogue?
text:
In November 2021, searches for a band that broke up in 1970 nearly tripled in a single week. I wanted to know one thing. Was that the documentary, or just Christmas?
The band is the Beatles. The documentary is Get Back, eight hours of restored 1969 footage that Peter Jackson dropped on Disney+ over three days, the 25th to the 27th of November. Google searches for the Beatles jumped to 2.7 times their normal level the same week.
Here is the trap. December always lifts music searches. Gifts, playlists, nostalgia, family. A simple before-and-after would hand the documentary a spike that partly belongs to the calendar. That is correlation wearing the costume of an effect, and it is the most common mistake in measurement.
So I ran a diff-in-diff. The idea is simple. Find things that ride the same seasonal wave but had no documentary, and let them tell you what the Beatles would have done anyway. My control group was three legacy bands with no shock in the window: the Rolling Stones, Led Zeppelin, Pink Floyd. If Christmas alone drove the spike, they should spike too.



Diff-in-diff chart of Google search trends before and after the Get Back documentary


They did not. Before Get Back, the four bands moved together closely enough to trust the comparison — that co-movement is the parallel trends assumption, and you can watch it hold in the chart. After the release, the Beatles shot up while the controls stayed flat. The distance between what happened and what the controls say would have happened is the causal effect: roughly 23 index points over the following eight weeks, a 63% lift the control bands never got.
Then the honest part. It faded. By January the Beatles were back near baseline. A documentary is a pulse, not a plateau. It buys a spike of attention, not a permanent shift in demand, and pretending otherwise is how people oversell a launch.
Now swap the documentary for an ad campaign. This is the single most common question I get asked to answer. Not “did the numbers go up after we spent the money,” but “did they go up because of it.” The gap between those two questions is worth a lot of budget, and diff-in-diff is one of the cleanest ways to close it. All it needs is a control group that shares your seasonality and skipped your treatment.
A note on the data. Google Trends is a search proxy, normalized 0 to 100, not stream counts. Three controls beat one because no single band’s noise can carry the result — I tested that: the Stones had their own shock in 2021, the death of Charlie Watts. Drop them entirely and the estimate moves from 23.5 to 22.2 points. The result survives losing a third of the control group. The design is the point, not the decimal.
So what would you have used as the control group?
Code and data: github.com/taniseb/beatlenomics

title: Which songs never retire?
text:
Some songs never leave a setlist. Others get played once and vanish forever. I wanted to know if there is a pattern, so I ran a survival analysis, the technique epidemiologists use to ask “how long until this patient relapses,” on Paul McCartney’s live rotation instead.
I sampled a full setlist from each of 12 tour eras, 1976 to 2024, one show per era, except the current one, where I pooled the six Got Back shows I have on record. Then I tracked every song: which era it first appeared in, and how many eras later it was still being played (or if it dropped out for good).
Split by origin, the pattern is clean. Twelve tour-eras after entering rotation, 41% of Beatles songs are still being played live. Of Wings and solo songs, 19%. A Beatles song that makes the setlist once is roughly twice as likely to still be there decades later.
This is not really about nostalgia. It is about catalogue depth: a much larger audience has a personal stake in a Beatles song than in almost any Wings or solo track, and that stake doesn’t decay the way an artist’s own new material does.
Every content library faces this. Some assets earn a permanent slot in rotation. Most don’t, no matter how good they are on release day.
What’s the “Beatles song” in your own portfolio, the thing that just doesn’t get retired?

title: The question streaming data can’t honestly answer
text:
The Beatles held out against streaming for years after Spotify launched. On 24 December 2015, at 12:01am local time, “here, there and everywhere,” the entire catalogue went live at once.
The obvious next question: what did the wait cost them in streams? I went looking for the data to answer that properly. Spotify does not publish a historical stream count by artist, not for the Beatles, not for anyone. There is no trajectory to fit a counterfactual against, only scattered numbers the press happened to capture: 6.5 million monthly listeners at the 100 day mark in 2016, “Here Comes the Sun” crossing 1 billion streams in May 2023, seven and a half years after entry.
I also wanted “early joiners” as a comparison. Led Zeppelin and Pink Floyd beat the Beatles to streaming, but by about two years. AC/DC, by six months. That is not a spectrum of early versus late. That is one cluster of legacy holdouts arriving within three years of each other.
So the honest post is not a number. It is this: the data to calculate “the cost of the holdout” simply does not exist in public form, for the Beatles or anyone else who waited. Every projection you have ever seen claiming to know that cost was built on an assumption nobody can verify.
What’s a number you’ve seen presented with total confidence that actually rests on data nobody has?

title: I saw Paul McCartney live 13 times
text:
I have seen Paul McCartney live 13 times. Porto Alegre, Rio de Janeiro twice in a row, Recife, Montevideo, Porto Alegre again, Buenos Aires, Mexico City, Brasilia, Curitiba, two nights in Sao Paulo, Florianopolis. Fourteen years, four countries, one guy who refuses to slow down.
So I did what I do. I pulled all 13 setlists and counted. Across 85 different songs he played for me over those years, only 12 showed up at every single show. Not once dropped, not once swapped out, across six different tours and a fourteen year gap between the first and the last.
Ob-La-Di, Ob-La-Da is one of the 12. It is my favorite Beatles song, and it turns out Paul agrees with a strange kind of consistency: he has opened himself to plenty of setlist chaos, deep cuts, tour-specific surprises, and this one just never leaves.
Twelve songs is a small, stubborn core inside a much bigger, ever-changing show. I know exactly which one is mine.
Which song would survive all your favorite artist’s setlists?

title: The placebo test
text:
On Monday I showed that a documentary made a band that broke up in 1970 nearly triple its Google searches. Today I tried to prove that finding was fake. Here is what happened.
A number is not trustworthy because you found it. It is trustworthy because you tried to break it and could not. That second step is the one most people skip, and it is the one that separates a serious analysis from a pretty chart.
So I ran the placebo test. My diff-in-diff said Get Back lifted Beatles searches by 23 index points. Fine. But what if my method just manufactures effects? What if it would find a lift anywhere I pointed it? There is a clean way to check. Point it at a moment when nothing happened.
I took the exact same model and moved the treatment date to 63 other weeks. Weeks with no documentary, no reunion, no news. If the method is honest, those fake dates should come back near zero. If it invents effects, they should light up like the real one did.



Placebo test chart comparing Beatles search trends to a control band


They came back near zero. All 63 of them clustered around no effect, while the real Get Back estimate sat more than nine standard deviations away, alone out in the tail. Not one fake date came close. Then I ran it the other way, pretending a control band was the treated one on the real release date. Near zero again. The effect refused to be faked, from every angle I tried.
Here is the lesson hiding inside the lesson. The only fake dates that showed anything at all were the ones parked right after the real spike, and those were not clean nulls — they were catching the tail of the true effect. A placebo is only as good as the window you give it. Run it carelessly and it will lie to you too.
Now take this out of music. It is the question to ask anyone who shows you a lift, from an ad campaign, a feature launch, a price cut. Not “how big was it.” Ask “did you run it where nothing happened, and did it come back empty.” If they never tried to break their own result, they do not have a result. They have a hope with a chart attached.
The job was never finding the effect. It was failing to destroy it.
So what is the last number you trusted that nobody stress-tested?

title: Who owns the Beatles?
text:
In 1963, Lennon and McCartney signed their songs to a company called Northern Songs. They were 22 and 21. By 1969, they had lost control of the catalogue entirely. By 1985, someone who never wrote a single Beatles song owned it.
I tracked every transaction. Here is what the ownership of the most valuable songbook in popular music looks like as a financial asset.
1963. Northern Songs is created. Lennon and McCartney are minority shareholders in their own work. Publisher Dick James and manager Brian Epstein hold the majority.
1969. After Epstein’s death, Dick James sells his shares to Lew Grade’s ATV for 1.5 million pounds, without telling Lennon or McCartney. The Beatles try to buy back control. They fail. They sell their remaining shares for 3.5 million pounds. ATV ends up with 92%. Total implied valuation of Northern Songs at the time of ATV’s bid: roughly 9.5 million pounds.
1985. Michael Jackson buys ATV Music for 47.5 million dollars. The catalogue contains about 4,000 songs. 251 of them are Lennon-McCartney compositions. That works out to roughly 11,900 dollars per song across the whole catalogue, or 189,000 dollars per Beatles song if you allocate the entire price to just the 251. McCartney wanted to buy it. He was outbid on his own songs.
1995. Facing financial pressure, Jackson merges the catalogue with Sony’s publishing arm. Sony/ATV is born. Jackson keeps 50%.
2016. Seven years after Jackson’s death, his estate sells the remaining 50% to Sony for 750 million dollars. The implied valuation of the full catalogue: 1.5 billion.



Timeline chart of Beatles song catalogue ownership changes


Now here is where it gets interesting for anyone who thinks about returns.
47.5 million in 1985 became 1.5 billion in 2016. That is a 31x increase in 31 years, which works out to 11.8% compound annual growth in nominal terms. Adjusted for inflation, the real return is about 8.9% per year.
How does that compare? The S&P 500 returned roughly 11.1% nominal over the same period. Gold returned 4.5%. US housing appreciated at about 3.5% annually in real terms.
So the Beatles catalogue performed roughly in line with the US stock market, beat gold by a wide margin, and crushed real estate. As an asset class, a songbook written by four men from Liverpool in the 1960s tracked the performance of the 500 largest American companies for three decades.
The price per song tells the story even more clearly. In 1985, each song in the ATV catalogue was worth about 11,900 dollars. By 2016, that same song was worth roughly 375,000 dollars. A 32x appreciation per composition.
But here is the part that still surprises me. In 2018, McCartney began using a provision in US copyright law that lets writers of pre-1978 songs reclaim their publishing rights after 56 years. He filed for 267 songs and reached a confidential settlement with Sony in 2017. More than fifty years after losing control, the law gave him a path back in.
The writers created the value. An investor captured the return. And eventually, a clause in copyright law did what no business negotiation could. That is the economics of intellectual property in one catalogue.

title: The McCartney Index, Brazil over time
text:
Same idea as the Big Mac Index, but pointed at one country over time instead of many countries at once. I priced the same kind of seat, the upper tier, for five Paul McCartney shows in Brazil across 13 years: 2011, 2012, 2017, 2023, 2024. What happened to that price, against minimum wage and against The Economist’s own Big Mac price for Brazil?
Indexed to 2011, by 2024: the ticket is up 150%. Minimum wage, up 159%. The Big Mac, up 152%. Paul’s ticket basically tracked a burger for thirteen years. No special McCartney inflation.
Except one year. In 2017, the ticket jumped to nearly double its 2011 price while wages and burgers were still under double. That’s the one year the show got relatively less affordable, and it corrected back in line by the next tour.
The lesson is not “concert prices are fine, don’t worry.” It is that a single snapshot (like the country comparison in the first McCartney Index post) can hide a story that only shows up over time: this market wasn’t drifting away from affordability, it had one bad year, priced in, and moved on.
What’s a price you assumed only goes up, that actually just tracks everything else?

title: My own McCartney Index
text:
I built the McCartney Index once already, comparing seven countries on the same tour. Then I realized I have my own version: four Paul McCartney shows, four different countries, four different tours, at whatever tier I actually bought.
Uruguay, 2014, standing floor: 3.5 days of local minimum wage. Mexico, 2023, standing floor: 5.7 days. Argentina, 2019, premium standing: 12.6 days. Brazil, 2024, premium standing: 21 days. Twenty one days of minimum wage for one night, in my own country.
This is not a clean experiment like the first index. Different tours, different years, different currencies moving at different speeds. Mexico’s ticket here is regular standing, not premium, because that’s what I actually bought that year. And I no longer have the receipts, so each number is the official box office price of my tier at the time, not a crumpled ticket stub. I am not pretending otherwise.
But that is also the point. The clean version tells you what the product costs. This one tells you what my own choices cost, premium standing almost every time, across a decade of chasing the same band around a continent, and there is a real gap in the middle: my personal ticket cost is a story of income too, not just of prices.
What’s your version of this, the thing you keep paying for at wildly different relative costs?

title: The McCartney Index
text:
The Economist has measured currencies with a hamburger since 1986. I measured with a beatle.
Same idea as the Big Mac Index: find one identical product sold in many countries, compare what it really costs in each. My product is the cheapest full price, unrestricted view ticket to Paul McCartney’s Got Back tour, same show, same stage, same setlist, in seven countries.
The headline is not the price tag. It is how many days of local minimum wage that ticket costs. In the US, 0.6 of a day. In Australia, Spain, France and the UK, under two days. In Mexico, 3.3 days. In Brazil, 9.6 days, about 15 times the US burden, for the same three hours of Hey Jude.
There is a PPP angle for the econ crowd too: the implied exchange rate from ticket prices says most currencies are undervalued against the dollar. But take that as directional only. Sales opened in different years (the US price is from 2022), so the price comparison mixes vintages, the classic measurement trap in any cross-country index. The days-of-wage number dodges it: each ticket is divided by the minimum wage in force on its own sale date.
Every global brand pricing the same product across borders is running this exact test, just with worse merch.
How many days of your own minimum wage would your favorite artist’s cheapest ticket cost?

title: The setlist is made of blocks
text:
A Paul McCartney show feels spontaneous, three hours, decades of catalogue, no visible script. I ran a cluster analysis on the 13 setlists I’ve seen him play and found the opposite: a stable structure of blocks.
Distance between two songs is how far apart, on average, they sit in the set. Cluster them and three clean, contiguous blocks fall out: an opening run of upbeat hits, a long acoustic and deep-cut middle, and a fixed emotional closing block, Let It Be through the Abbey Road medley.
The closing block is the rigid one. Golden Slumbers, Carry That Weight and The End moved less than 5.3% of the set’s length across 13 shows spanning 14 years. Three other songs (A Day in the Life, Paperback Writer, I’ve Got a Feeling) never found a stable slot at all, swinging from the opener to the encore depending on the night, and that inconsistency is exactly what proves the other blocks are real.
He isn’t swapping songs. He’s swapping modules, and one module never moves.
Any product built from swappable modules works the same way: some pieces are up for reshuffling, and one or two are load bearing.
Which part of your own routine never moves, no matter what else changes around it?

title: Concentration in Paul McCartney’s setlists
text:
Paul McCartney has played 373 different songs live. Half of them account for 1% of his stage time.
I pulled his full live history, every documented show, 30,369 performances in total, and looked at how it distributes. It is one of the most lopsided catalogues I have ever measured.
The numbers are blunt. 117 songs got played exactly once. Almost half the catalogue shows up five times or fewer. The median song has been played six times in his entire career. And the top 50 songs carry 68% of every performance.



Chart showing concentration of Paul McCartney’s live setlist across 373 songs


Put it on a Lorenz curve and the Gini comes out at 0.77. I measure market concentration for a living, and that number is higher than the income inequality of any country on earth.
There is an era story underneath it. The Beatles years lasted about eight. His solo and Wings career runs past fifty. Yet Beatles songs still take 65% of his stage time. Eight years of output drive two thirds of what he plays. Supply and demand point in opposite directions.
This is demand concentration, the same shape that runs through streaming, publishing, and box office. A few legacy assets carry the whole catalogue, and anything new has to compete with a back catalogue that never depreciates. People do not pay for the newest song. They pay for the one that became canon.
The uncomfortable part, if you build anything creative, is that your catalogue’s value does not spread evenly across what you make. It clusters, hard. The real question is not how much you produce. It is whether you ever make another thing that climbs into the head of the curve.
My favourite Beatles song, Ob-La-Di Ob-La-Da, sits in the top 6%. Good company, as it turns out.
A note on the data. This comes from publicly documented setlists on setlist.fm. The counts are fan logged, so read them as floors, not exact totals. The Gini is computed across all 373 songs.
So what is your read. Is McCartney leaving money on the table by underplaying fifty years of solo work, or is giving people the hits simply the rational move?
Code and data: github.com/taniseb/beatlenomics

title: If Paul’s setlist were a market
text:
By day I compute HHIs for merger review. I pointed the same formula at Paul McCartney’s live setlist.
Treat each songwriting era as a firm competing for setlist slots: Beatles, Wings, solo and covers. Share of slots squared and summed gives the HHI, the standard concentration measure regulators use, on a 0 to 10,000 scale.
Every single tour era on record, 1976 to 2024, sits above 2,500, the threshold authorities call highly concentrated. Not trending up. Already there in 1976, when Wings held 76% of the set. What changes is who holds the dominant position. By 1989, Wings had collapsed to 7% and the Beatles catalogue took over at 57%. In 2024, Beatles hold 61%, HHI at 4,519, well past the line where a real market gets a hard look.
No regulator would approve this. The dominant firm dissolved in 1970 and has released essentially no new product in fifty years, one 2023 single aside, and it still gained share for three decades.
What market in your own life would fail a concentration test if you ran the numbers?

title: The geo-lift that broke on contact with the data
text:
Paul McCartney played 5 cities on the 2023 Brazil leg of his Got Back tour. For a causal inference person, that looks like a natural experiment: treated markets with a show, untreated markets without one.
So I built the geo-lift test. Google Trends for “Paul McCartney,” weekly, at state level as a proxy for each host city: Brasília, Belo Horizonte, São Paulo, Curitiba, Rio de Janeiro as treated, Salvador, Recife, Fortaleza, Porto Alegre, Manaus as control, no show in any of them.
The design broke on the first look at the chart. Search interest in host cities peaked at 8.8x their own baseline during the tour. Cities with NO show surged right alongside them, and matched that peak exactly, 8.8x their own baseline too, one week later as the tour closed.
The control group moved almost in lockstep with the treatment. A 5-city tour through a country this size is national news. It leads entertainment segments, trends on social media, gets talked about in cities Paul never visited. The “control” markets were never isolated from the treatment. They caught the same national wave, just a beat later.
This is the failure mode every geo-lift practitioner has to check before trusting a lift number: is your control market actually insulated from the campaign, or does it just look untouched because nobody measured the spillover? Big enough events break the geography the test depends on.
What would you have used as an untouched control here?

title: Now and Then: the halo effect on the catalogue
text:
In 2023 the Beatles released a new song. The interesting question is not how it charted. It is what it did to searches for everything else they ever recorded.
“Now and Then” came out on 2 November 2023, billed as the last new Beatles track, built from a decades-old Lennon demo. I pulled Google Trends for “The Beatles” against three legacy bands with no shock in the window (Stones, Zeppelin, Pink Floyd) and ran the same diff-in-diff from my Get Back post.
First surprise: attention started moving a full week before there was anything to hear. The teaser and the announcement, with not a note of music released yet, lifted searches about 30% off baseline. The peak week bundles the short film and the release itself, so the cleanest evidence that promotion moves people is that pre-release jump, before the product existed publicly.
Second surprise: the effect after release was roughly half of Get Back’s. But it did not fully fade. Three months out, Beatles search interest was still above where the pre-launch trend put it, while the control bands sat flat. A new song, even one built from an old cassette, left a longer afterglow on the whole catalogue than an 8-hour documentary did.
Product launches work the same way. An iPhone announcement starts moving people well before launch day, and the halo on the rest of the product line often outlasts both.
What lifts your back catalogue more, the trailer or the thing itself?

title: It never gets old. But does it never get old?
text:
The Beatles sold 600 million records. The best-selling act in music history, by a wide margin.
On Spotify, they have about 26 billion total streams and roughly 10 million monthly listeners. Taylor Swift has over 100 billion streams and 103 million monthly listeners. The Beatles are not in the top 50 most-streamed artists on the platform. They are not even the most-streamed classic rock band. That title goes to Queen, with 29 billion streams and 50 million monthly listeners.
So when we say the Beatles never get old, what exactly are we measuring? I ran the numbers three different ways.
First, sales per year of active career. The Beatles were together for seven years, 1963 to 1970. In that window, they sold 600 million records — 86 million per year. Elvis, over a 23-year career, averaged 22 million per year. Taylor Swift, across 18 years, averages about 11 million per year. By annual output rate, the Beatles are not just the biggest. They operated at 4x the pace of Elvis and 8x the pace of Taylor Swift.
Second, streams per original song. The Beatles recorded roughly 213 original compositions. Their 26 billion Spotify streams spread across those tracks give an average of about 122 million streams per song. Queen, with approximately 180 songs and 29 billion streams, averages 162 million per song — a higher per-song streaming density. Part of the explanation is “Bohemian Rhapsody,” which got a second life from the 2018 film and sits at over 2 billion streams alone.



Chart comparing Beatles streaming numbers to other classic rock acts


Third, the time disadvantage. The Beatles catalogue was not available on any streaming platform until December 24, 2015. That means their 26 billion streams were accumulated in roughly 10 years, not the 18 years Spotify has existed — about 2.5 billion plays per year. Taylor Swift’s is about 6.7 billion per year, a 2.7 to 1 ratio. Significant, but smaller than the 10 to 1 gap in monthly listeners would suggest.
And then there is “Here Comes the Sun.” Written by George Harrison in 1969. It has 1.8 billion Spotify streams — the first song from the 1960s to cross one billion plays on any streaming platform. It averages roughly 472,000 plays per day, every day, 57 years after it was recorded. No algorithmic playlist strategy, no TikTok campaign, no coordinated release. Just a track that people keep pressing play on.
Here is what the data actually says. The Beatles dominated an era when success meant selling a physical object. Streaming measures something different: not the decision to buy, but the decision to listen again. Sales are a stock metric — they accumulate and never go down. Streams are a flow metric — they measure ongoing, current demand.
By the stock metric, no one will ever catch the Beatles. 600 million records in seven years is a number that belongs to a format that no longer exists. By the flow metric, they are a mid-tier legacy act on Spotify, outperformed by Queen, by Coldplay, by artists who are still releasing music and feeding the algorithm.
But 472,000 daily plays of a 1969 track is not nostalgia. That is a song that still solves a problem for listeners, 57 years later. The catalogue ages. The best songs do not.
Greatest ever? Almost certainly. Most listened to right now? Not even close. That gap is the most honest thing data can tell you about how culture ages.
Code and data: github.com/taniseb/beatlenomics

title: Bohemian Rhapsody & synthetic control
text:
In November 2018, Queen’s streams exploded. Everyone knows why. Almost nobody can say by how much.
“By how much” needs a baseline, and “before the movie” is the wrong one. The right baseline is a Queen that never had a movie at all.
So I built one. A synthetic Queen, a weighted mix of legacy bands with no shock that year, mostly Pink Floyd, some Rolling Stones, picked because that mix matched real Queen best before the premiere. Real Queen ran about 1.4x above synthetic Queen for sixteen weeks after release.
Then I ran the placebo check from my last post on every control. Three came back clean. One did not: Pink Floyd rose too in that window, and Pink Floyd is 65% of my synthetic Queen. But notice which way that cuts. If my control rose on its own, my baseline is too high, and 1.4x is a floor, not a ceiling. Rebuild the synthetic without Pink Floyd and the lift climbs to 1.79x, on a worse pre-movie fit. I will take the conservative number.
Swap the movie for an ad campaign and this is the exact question incrementality testing answers, placebo included.
Which control would you have trusted least?

title: Launching #beatlenomics
text:
I started a side project this weekend, and it has almost nothing to do with my day job. Almost.
My work is measuring how concentrated markets are. Who holds the power, how unevenly value is spread, what the numbers say when the official story says something else. Last week it hit me that I could point the exact same tools at something I actually love. The Beatles.
So I am starting #beatlenomics. Short essays where I take one question about The Beatles or Paul McCartney, pull real data, and answer it with a chart and one economic idea. No nostalgia for its own sake. Just the numbers, and what they quietly reveal about how cultural value works.
The first one looks at Paul’s live shows. I compiled his full performance history, 373 different songs, and the distribution turned out more unequal than the income of any country on earth.
I am keeping the whole thing open. The code, the data, and the charts live on GitHub. If you want to see how it is built, or borrow the approach for your own data, it is all there.
This is the part of data work I enjoy most. Taking a method built for serious questions and letting it loose on something joyful.
What would you want measured about a band you love?

title: Paul at 80+, still touring
text:
Paul McCartney turned 80 in 2022 and kept touring. I wondered if that showed up in the one number that’s hardest to fake on stage: how many songs he actually plays.
I went back to the 13 shows I’ve seen him play, from Porto Alegre in 2010 (he was 68) to Sao Paulo in 2024 (he was 82), and counted the setlist every time.
Average setlist before he turned 80: 37 songs. At 80 or older: 40. No decline. If anything, a small bump, and his longest set in the data (43 songs) came at 81, in Brasilia.
One honest caveat, because it changes what the number means: my pre-80 shows span six different tours, and every single one of my 80+ shows is the same tour, Got Back. So this is really “the current tour did not get shorter,” not “age has no effect.” I only have the shows I went to.
Even read that narrowly, it is striking. Most performers taper, and the tapering usually shows up as a shorter set first. He is running the same show length, in the same three-hour range, more than a decade past when most careers wind down.
Maybe the real product was never “young Paul.” It was reliability. Same effort, show after show, decade after decade, and the market keeps paying full price for it.
What’s the oldest you’ve seen a performer keep their full act intact?
